item.title: Can Australian businesses legally ban customers from using smart glasses?
item.description: Businesses and local councils around Australia are increasingly imposing their own restrictions on "smart glasses," responding to customers' concerns about being covertly recorded in public places. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dual-purpose qubit design could speed operations while cutting quantum errors
item.description: Researchers from MIT have designed a new qubit architecture that enables qubits to interact with each other much more quickly while remaining very stable. This advance could someday help scientists build practical quantum computers that can run long, complex algorithms with high accuracy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Heat has a memory—and a new theoretical framework can track it
item.description: Heat, it turns out, has a memory. A cooling cup of coffee may not seem particularly thoughtful. At the scale of a kitchen, heat appears to follow a straightforward rule: it moves from warmer places to cooler ones. Leave the cup unattended long enough, and the disappointing result offers convincing evidence that this rule works. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: First DDT, now the flu: Peregrine falcons in San Francisco Bay Area hit hard by H5N1 variant
item.description: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) featured prominently in the news during 2020 as it took the lives of millions of birds across the globe. While the worst seems to be behind us, population-level effects are just now emerging. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Who hears you say 'thank you?' It matters more than you might think
item.description: There are many ways to say thank you. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Quantum control algorithm looks to explain how birds migrate
item.description: The hidden world of quantum mechanics exists at scales many orders of magnitude smaller than living organisms, yet scientists have long theorized that quantum effects play an important role in biology. Birds' ability to sense magnetic fields during migration is one of the best-known mysteries in this field, with leading theories suggesting that this sensing could be achieved by exploiting quantum entanglement. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why feeding birds can make you feel better
item.description: More than 56 million U.S. adults feed wild birds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Hubble Spies Superbubble Scene
item.description: This Hubble Space Telescope image features a sprawling cosmic vista called N44. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Ancient “living fossils” may reveal how complex life began
item.description: A newly discovered microbe living inside ancient stromatolite communities may offer a rare look at how complex life first emerged. Researchers captured the first direct images of an Asgard archaeon physically connected to a bacterium, with the two microbes appearing to exchange nutrients and other compounds. Scientists think similar partnerships billions of years ago may have helped produce the first complex cells. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Overqualification can make or break family life, study reveals
item.description: New research shows overqualified employees who prioritize work over family are more likely to let anxiety and fear about their careers spill into their home lives, creating damaging conflict. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA scientists discover a giant 10-sided pattern on Saturn
item.description: A huge 10-sided atmospheric pattern has appeared around Saturn’s south pole, giving the planet a surprising counterpart to its famous northern hexagon. Hubble data suggest the strange decagon only began emerging in the past few years and is still growing stronger. Researchers hope continued observations will reveal why it suddenly formed and whether it could persist for decades. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Can an AI tutor help students improve at math?
item.description: As schools contend with rapid developments in artificial intelligence, new research from the University of Toronto Mississauga suggests an AI tutor could help students with math, but only if it holds back answers and coaches them through problems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When panic freezes people: Virtual quake tests capture real-time fear and injury risk
item.description: Growing up, many of us were taught to drop, cover and hold on during an earthquake. The guidance is straightforward, but how people actually respond when the ground starts shaking can be far more complicated. Now, UC Berkeley researchers are studying what happens in those critical moments and how fear and risk perception influence people's actions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In 1999, scientists dropped 45 tons of wollastonite over a 29-acre New Hampshire watershed
item.description: In an ambitious forest restoration initiative in New Hampshire, researchers sought to mitigate the effects of acid rain. They introduced calcium-rich minerals, leading to an initial boost in tree vitality and growth. However, this solution inadvertently resulted in a staggering increase in nitrogen levels in nearby streams, releasing thirty times more inorganic nitrogen compared to untreated regions. This outcome underscores the intricate dynamics of ecosystems in response to human intervention. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: The biggest black hole merger ever observed could be less massive than it appears
item.description: Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime created when pairs of black holes spiral into each other and eventually merge. But if this ripple has been warped by another massive object on its way to Earth, a new analysis suggests that these black holes might appear far larger than they really are. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Our pay is called a 'salary,' but were Roman soldiers really paid in salt?
item.description: Every other Wednesday, like clockwork, my salary arrives in my bank account. By Thursday, most of it is gone. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists just overturned a century-old physics assumption
item.description: Scientists at Carnegie Mellon University have discovered an unexpected form of the Hall effect, overturning the long-held assumption that this electrical response only appears when a magnetic field points perpendicular to a material. Beyond expanding a century-old principle of physics, the finding could eventually lead to simpler magnetic sensors for electronics, transportation, and medical technologies. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Looking back to forecast the future of lobster
item.description: For generations, the lobster fishery has been central to the cultural and economic identity of Maine and Atlantic Canada. Predicting what the future holds for the species—and the people who depend on it—has long been a priority for scientists and resource managers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bats carry dangerous viruses without getting sick. This may be why
item.description: Scientists discovered that more than 500 species of vesper bats possess two separate sets of antibody genes, an immune arrangement never before found in mammals. The surprising system could help explain how bats tolerate so many viruses without becoming seriously ill. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Salt may have helped turn Earth into a frozen world 700 million years ago
item.description: Earth may have been pushed deeper into a global deep freeze by something surprisingly ordinary: salt. Around 700 million years ago, Earth entered periods of extreme glaciation known as Snowball Earth, when ice is thought to have spread across much or potentially all of the planet's surface. Scientists have long known that expanding ice could have helped drive this transition: As bright ice replaces darker ocean water, more sunlight is reflected back into space, causing the planet to cool further and allowing even more ice to form. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Teenage kicks: Why Australian youth culture must be preserved
item.description: From the rock 'n' roll and punk scenes, soda fountains and graduation-week celebrations, surfers, skaters, ravers and the modern-day Eshay, generations of young Australians have been creating culture, but much of it risks disappearing from the historical record. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Informal supporters share experiences of NDIS behavior support practitioners
item.description: A new national survey of informal supporters of people with disabilities who have received NDIS-funded behavior support services has identified wide variation in supporters' confidence in practitioners' knowledge and skills, pointing to a need for greater transparency about practitioner expertise and stronger, more consistent, rights-based behavior support across the NDIS. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why Britons disagree about poverty: They draw the line differently
item.description: People with different political beliefs do not only disagree about how much poverty exists in Britain but they also differ over whether the same material circumstances should be defined as poverty, according to new research from the University of Bath School of Management. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: One immune switch may help drive aging across the body
item.description: Aging may be partly fueled by immune cells losing their ability to clear away damaged, inflammation-promoting cells. Blocking a single receptor restored that cleanup process in mice, reducing inflammation and helping their organs, muscles, and memory remain remarkably youthful. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Los últimos mensajes de la pareja italiana que mató a su hija discapacitada y luego se suicidó: "Escribamos en el grupo y nos echamos unas risas"
item.description: Los forenses practican las autopsias y el test de la parafina a la pareja hallada muerta junto a su hija de cinco años en Roma, mientras los investigadores intentan esclarecer la mecánica exacta del crimen a partir de la pistola Glock incautada en la vivienda Leer Fuente: El Mundo - Internacional.

item.description: After eight years of travelling through the inner Solar System, BepiColombo is arriving at Mercury. This page will show the latest updates throughout the mission's arrival. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Electron spin unlocks magnetic control of hydrogen surface reactions
item.description: Chemical reactions at surfaces play a central role in many processes, including catalysis and materials synthesis. It is well known that the outcome of these reactions is influenced by the translational, vibrational and rotational motions of atoms and molecules. Now, a study shows that electron spin, another fundamental property of matter, also influences how chemical reactions at surfaces unfold. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Heavy water's atmospheric fingerprints boost weather forecasts for up to five days
item.description: Weather forecasts rely on many different kinds of data, including temperature, humidity and wind. For the first time, researchers, including those at the University of Tokyo, have demonstrated that a long-theorized improvement to weather models—adding data on water isotopes in the atmosphere—does work. They showed that incorporating satellite measurements of water vapor isotopes into weather models improves forecasts of atmospheric conditions for up to five days, including predictions of heavy rainfall in many regions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In 2010, US scientists tracked dye 41.2 miles in Montana’s Missouri River; a reservoir held it 8.2 hours
item.description: Scientists conducted a dye-tracing experiment on Montana's Missouri River. This study examined how substances move through the waterway over forty miles. The dye traveled at different speeds through various river sections and reservoirs. Researchers measured how the dye plume spread along the river's direction. This data aids in predicting contaminant movement and planning for accidental spills. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: AI boom is testing tech firms' climate pledges
item.description: Technology companies are stepping up their climate commitments but not fast enough to counter rapidly growing energy needs linked to the artificial intelligence boom, a report said Wednesday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In Chile, injured penguins sport copper vests to help them heal
item.description: Researchers in Chile have designed an unlikely new garment for injured penguins—snug red vests threaded with copper and zinc that they hope will help the aquatic birds heal faster. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Underwater meadows sustain millions in extreme poverty
item.description: A study provides the first large-scale empirical evidence that seagrass meadows act as a critical safety net for millions of coastal people living in extreme poverty across the Indo-Pacific. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Christina Koch, astronauta de Artemis II: “La respuesta a nuestra misión aquí en la Tierra superó con creces todo lo que habíamos imaginado y esperado”
item.description: Tras su regreso a la Tierra, Donald Trump le entregó a cada tripulante una medalla Medalla de Honor Espacial del Congreso, durante una ceremonia en el Centro Espacial Jonhson de Houston Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: The universe has plenty of hydrogen. So why is star formation collapsing?
item.description: Star formation across the universe has fallen dramatically over the past 4.5 billion years, but astronomers have uncovered a surprising twist: the supply of neutral hydrogen, a key ingredient for making stars, has barely declined. Using China’s FAST radio telescope and data from roughly 2.5 million galaxies observed by DESI, researchers found that star formation was about 2.5 times higher 4.5 billion years ago, while neutral hydrogen levels were only about 1.4 times higher. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: September brings a dazzling Venus and a glowing Harvest Moon
item.description: September’s sky features brilliant Venus, the Milky Way’s hazy center, and the seasonal turning point of the equinox. The month ends with a glowing Harvest Moon rising near Saturn and faint Neptune. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: La mala noticia es que el oxígeno de la Tierra tiene fecha de caducidad. La buena es que no estaremos aquí para verlo
item.description: Podemos respirar tranquilos. También los nietos de los nietos de nuestros nietos. Pero el oxígeno que sustenta la vida compleja en la Tierra no será eterno. A nuestra atmósfera rica en oxígeno le quedan, aproximadamente, mil millones de años . Entonces, el cambio será drástico. Una desoxigenación rápida. Después de hacer más de 400.000 simulaciones sobre la evolución geológica y biológica de nuestro planeta, científicos japoneses y estadounidenses llegaron a la conclusión de que la Tierra experimentará una… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: Has Iran modified its rocket systems to fire mines into the Strait of Hormuz?
item.description: Fighting escalated in the Middle East over the weekend after US airstrikes on Sunday targeted Iranian rocket launchers on the island of Larak. The exchange of fire was instigated by the US in retaliation against Iran’s new capabilities for firing mines from rockets into the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s use of rocket launchers to deploy sea mines into the strategic waterway would be unprecedented, but not implausible. Even so, some analysts remain sceptical. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: Sébastian SEIBT

item.title: Hong Kong considers DNA testing amid concerns over ‘fighting dog’ classification
item.description: Hong Kong authorities are considering genetic testing as a supplementary tool for identifying breeds, an official has said after enforcement action against suspected fighting dogs sparked public concern. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) also said on Thursday that owners could keep existing fighting dogs, provided they complied with statutory requirements, and urged owners not to abandon their pets. Dr Michelle Yeung Lee, the department’s principal veterinary officer,... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Leopold Chen

item.title: Biodegradable 'nanobone' could one day help regrow bone without painful grafts
item.description: For children born with cleft lip and palate, repairing gaps in the jawbone often means waiting until they are 10 to 12 years old before undergoing invasive bone graft surgery. University of Sydney researchers have developed a biodegradable "nanobone" material that allows the body to harness its own healing properties to regrow bone, offering a potential future alternative to procedures that have changed little in more than 50 years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: With education technology, engagement is not the same as learning
item.description: A new report from the American Psychological Association warns that student engagement with educational technology is not the same as learning—and that generative AI tools pose particular risks by improving students' immediate performance without building their underlying knowledge or skills. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: ADHD may have a surprising creative advantage
item.description: Some of the attention patterns that make ADHD challenging may also help spark creativity by allowing the brain to explore more ideas and unexpected connections. Researchers think creative activities could potentially channel this “defocused attention” while helping strengthen the brain systems involved in focus and self-control. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Study reveals distinct patterns across single-, multi-, and mass homicides
item.description: An updated analysis of U.S. homicide data has found that intimate partner violence (IPV) often precipitates mass homicide and is also frequently associated with multi-victim and single-victim deaths. The study categorizes homicides into single-victim, multi-victim (2–3 victims) and mass (4 or more victims, excluding the perpetrator) fatalities, revealing distinct demographics and circumstances. The findings of the study published in Annals of Epidemiology, can help inform the development of tailored strategies to prevent homicide. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Each extra hour of prolonged sitting linked to 9% higher cancer death risk
item.description: Sitting for long, uninterrupted stretches may carry greater health risks than sitting the same amount of time in shorter bouts. Researchers found that each extra hour of prolonged sedentary behavior was associated with a 9% higher risk of cancer death. Breaking up sitting with movement showed the opposite pattern, while replacing an hour of prolonged sitting with light activity was linked to a 12% lower risk. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Australia’s new environmental protection agency approves coal project, angering climate groups

The confirmation of the extension of the Saraji mine, which digs and exports coal for steel making, comes after the prime… Publicado también por: The Guardian - Environment. Fuente: The Guardian - World.

item.title: Crash in dugong population estimates, a warning sign governments can't ignore
item.description: A 50% decline in the Gulf of Carpentaria dugong population estimate is a wake-up call for urgent action to protect dugongs in the Gulf, based on surveys undertaken by researchers from James Cook University, Charles Darwin University and Indigenous Ranger groups. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: China launches largest-ever academic misconduct crackdown after ‘Student Geng’ scrutiny
item.description: Four Chinese academics who lost posts at leading universities after a high-profile blogger flagged their research for misconduct have come under official investigation by China’s leading funder of basic research. The National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) published details on August 26 of 31 new misconduct cases at universities and hospitals across China, involving more than 40 researchers – its largest such public disclosure to date. Among them were four prominent professors... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Pacific islands to face food shortages due to global warming: Scientists
item.description: The Pacific islands will face food shortages, and drinking water will be affected by rising seas, scientists said Wednesday, as a U.N. report found the world would fail to limit global warming to 1.5°C. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Immune therapy engineered inside the body eases multiple sclerosis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 03 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02765-1 Results from a small trial suggest a modified virus can instruct the immune system to wipe out disease-causing cells. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Rachel Fieldhouse

item.title: Five-metal 2D catalysts could convert CO₂ to CO without needing an extra electrical boost
item.description: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is usually discussed as something the world needs to get rid of. Activities such as the burning of fossil fuels for daily use, including electricity and transportation, and industrial applications release significant amounts of CO₂, and the gas enters the atmosphere. Researchers are now asking whether this road could have a roundabout. What if CO₂, which is at the center of the climate crisis, could be turned into something useful and put back into the industrial cycle? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cellular maintenance crew may miss as much as half of certain misfolded proteins
item.description: As proteins are made in a cell, they are folded into the 3D structure that allows them to work, but sometimes this process can go wrong. When it does, the misfolded proteins lose some or all of their function and usually get tagged by the cell's quality assurance and maintenance crews, which try to repair the proteins or, if they can't, strip them to recycle their parts. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Caterpillar twitches in an ultraquiet chamber help biologists understand how these insects hear without ears
item.description: In a quiet summer garden, a caterpillar perches on a branch, munching serenely on leaves. A moment later, it freezes. It senses danger—and just in time. From behind, a wasp approaches, sizing up its prey. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Trees use a 'muscle' to correct their posture—a newly discovered role for tension wood
item.description: A research team from INRAE and the University Clermont Auvergne has shown that trees are capable of correcting a curvature they detect in their stems through a specific biological process. In the study, young trees with bent stems were placed in an experimental set-up that prevented them from sensing their orientation relative to light and gravity. The only sense remaining to the trees was the perception of their own curvature. Under these conditions, the scientists observed the formation of a particular type of wood, known as tension wood, which acts like a muscle to correct the curvature of… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Trapped light generates nanoscale magnetization
item.description: Using an engineered metasurface that traps light, Cornell researchers have demonstrated a new way to generate strong static magnetic fields without using external magnets or magnetic materials—an approach that could advance spintronics, quantum and photonic computing, and data storage. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Copper's oxygen-rich early oxidation layer could inform catalyst design and nuclear waste storage
item.description: Copper roofs lose their reddish color over time because a pale green layer of copper oxide forms on their surface, protecting the roof from further corrosion for many years. But what exactly happens during the first steps of this process? Might it even be possible to stop it? This question has become increasingly urgent since copper containers have come to be regarded as one of the best options for storing nuclear waste. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Europe facing housing affordability crisis, continental study of more than 22 million property listings suggests
item.description: Nearly half of people living in Europe on an average income can only afford to buy the equivalent of a one-bedroom apartment or studio apartment, while 39% of Europeans cannot afford to rent a property this size. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI-designed proteins enable a new generation of RNA transporters
item.description: RNA-based therapeutics use RNA as a blueprint that enables cells to produce specific proteins—including proteins that can precisely modify genes. For this to work, the RNA must reach the inside of the cell intact. Delivery systems currently used for this purpose include virus-derived vehicles and lipid nanoparticles, tiny particles made of fat-like molecules. Both approaches have limitations. Researchers are therefore working on new mechanisms that can deliver RNA into cells more efficiently and, in the future, more selectively. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fish dads offer new insight into behavioral effects of receiving paternal care
item.description: The plot of "Finding Nemo," a film that features an overprotective single father fish taking on dangers at sea to care for his son, may be more reflective of actual fish dad behavior than was previously known. A new study led by a scientist at Penn State found that baby freshwater fish, when raised by dutiful fathers, fare far better than their non-dad-raised peers in life-or-death situations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Making superconductors thinner can change how they accommodate magnetic fields
item.description: What happens when a superconductor becomes so thin that electrons can no longer behave as if they were moving through an ordinary three-dimensional piece of metal? This question has been at the center of my recent work on quantum confinement in metallic films. Over the past few years, I have been developing this line of theory with my colleague Giovanni Ummarino at Politecnico di Torino. Our initial goal was to understand something rather concrete: Why does shrinking the thickness of a superconducting film change the temperature at which superconductivity appears? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists removed 285,000 fish from a Wisconsin lake to help walleye, but perch rose 788% instead
item.description: Scientists removed about 285,000 centrarchid fish from Wisconsin’s McDermott Lake between 2018 and 2021 to see if reducing competition and predation could help walleye recover. The experiment sharply reduced several fish species and saw yellow perch numbers rise by about 788%. However, researchers found no detectable natural walleye recruitment, showing that removing centrarchids alone did not restore the lake’s walleye population. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Hidden DNA in medieval gospels reveals history of deadly livestock virus
item.description: Some of Europe's most well-known historic manuscripts, including the York Gospels, have proven to be biological time capsules for uncovering the 3,500-year history of the sheeppox virus (SPPV). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Harnessing gold nanorods and light for targeted cancer therapy
item.description: One of the major challenges in the quest to beat cancer is developing treatments that can selectively destroy cancer cells while leaving healthy cells unharmed. With this in mind, researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar (IITGN) have devised a gold nanorod-based platform that delivers therapeutic agents specifically to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), a structure responsible for protein production and processing within cells, while also generating heat when exposed to near-infrared light. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: PACMAN AI framework for controlling fusion systems safely makes key decisions in milliseconds
item.description: Inside some fusion energy systems, particles hotter than the core of the sun can become unruly in a few thousandths of a second, far faster than any human operator can react. A new software framework developed by researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL) and Princeton University hands those split-second decisions to artificial intelligence (AI), while keeping the machine safe and humans firmly in charge of the goals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NYC, the nation's largest school system, bans AI for students through 8th grade
item.description: New York City's public schools will temporarily ban elementary and middle school students from using artificial intelligence tools during the upcoming school year, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Wednesday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tracing the legal history of the kiss—from property and contracts to consent
item.description: Is a kiss just a kiss? Or is it a sign of love, affection, a biological urge, a contract or even an assault? Law, history, evolution and anthropology show that it can be all those things. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hubble tracks new decagon encircling Saturn's south pole
item.description: Recent observations with NASA's Hubble Space Telescope have revealed a giant, evolving, 10-sided atmospheric wave encircling Saturn's south pole. This discovery marks the first time a large, regular-sided jet pattern has been observed in the planet's southern hemisphere. The feature appears remarkably similar to Saturn's famous hexagon at its north pole but is also distinctly different, suggesting scientists may be witnessing a new atmospheric phenomenon developing on the iconic gas giant. Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What's in an 'O'? Unusual Greek spelling may unlock mystery of ring tied to Pontius Pilate
item.description: It's a small, simple ring made of copper alloy and engraved with a handful of Greek letters and the image of a pottery vessel. But its unremarkable appearance belies a remarkable history: The signet was likely connected in some way to the New Testament figure Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea during the life of Jesus. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient fossil from China reveals animal‑microbe partnerships dating back 550 million years
item.description: We often think of microbes as organisms that live around us, like the Salmonella bacteria and flu viruses that cause illness. But some of our most intimate relationships are with the microbes living inside us. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New model explains how bacterial promoter elements set gene activity and regulation
item.description: Bacterial promoters are DNA sequences that recruit RNA polymerase to initiate transcription, primarily through two elements called −10 and −35. However, the contributions of these elements to promoter evolution and regulation have remained unclear. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Pac-Man' enzyme breaks down bioplastics and penicillin in laboratory tests
item.description: In the ocean, plastic waste collects to form large garbage patches that endanger marine life. This is partly because the synthetic plastic polymers used today can only be broken down biologically—that is, by microorganisms—at a very slow rate. Instead, the physical fragmentation of these materials leads to the formation of microplastics and nanoplastics. However, microorganisms do colonize plastic waste in the environment, forming biofilms and creating a unique microbial habitat that researchers refer to as the "plastisphere." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cluster's final reentry strengthens data for safer, more sustainable satellite design
item.description: The Cluster mission danced its final dance as Tango reentered the atmosphere Sept. 1 at 11:30:31 p.m. CEST. The end of the Cluster mission in 2024 marked the start of the reentry data-collection campaign. After four targeted reentries, this is now a proven method of safe end-of-life disposal. It also enabled repeated observation of the reentries by a plane full of scientists, creating a unique reentry data set that will improve our understanding of the destructive process and inform the design of safer, more sustainable satellites in the future. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Global road map tracks four years of infrastructure change using AI
item.description: The United Nations considers well-developed and safe roads an important part of infrastructure in its Sustainable Development Goals. Until now, however, there has been no benchmark for the condition and state of road networks worldwide. Researchers at the Institute of Geography at Heidelberg University and HeiGIT (Heidelberg Institute of Geoinformation Technology) have addressed this gap by using artificial intelligence and satellite imagery to create an open-access dataset that maps and classifies more than 9 million kilometers of roads worldwide. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: "Requirements are being adjusted to reflect near-term mission needs." Fuente: Ars Technica.

item.title: Quick action needed as the world is set to get hotter than we hoped
item.description: Global temperature rise is set to cross 1.5°C, likely within the next few years, pushing climate risks and impacts to increasingly dangerous heights. But it is still possible to bring temperatures down and achieve the global goals of the Paris Agreement, according to a new UN Environment Programme (UNEP) report. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Blind spots at Antarctic coasts limit sea level projections
item.description: The Antarctic coastal zone is not simply the edge of the continent. It is a tightly coupled system where ice from the ice sheet extends over the seabed, initially resting on it and farther out floating as ice shelves. Here, mass, heat and nutrients are exchanged with the ocean through various processes. Even the smallest changes can have outsized consequences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Revamps Challenge Linking Community College Studies to Aerospace Careers
item.description: Community college students across the U.S. now have another opportunity to discover how their education can lead to fulfilling roles at the forefront of aerospace, science, engineering, and technology. The updated NASA Community College Aerospace Scholars (NCAS) student challenge invites students to learn about the agency and its missions, engage with NASA experts, and explore […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: World must prepare for 'reality' of missing 1.5C goal: UN
item.description: The United Nations said Wednesday the 1.5°C target would be missed and outlined how global temperatures might be brought back down in a first-of-its-kind assessment met with dismay in climate-vulnerable nations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: US politics is not the world's template for polarization, experts warn
item.description: Common global narratives about political polarization are skewed because of an overreliance on literature about the U.S., leaving governments unprepared to tackle the problem at home. In new research led by King's College London and published in Nature Communications, experts across the U.K., Europe, Asia, Australia and the U.S. point to how common narratives about polarization are overgeneralized and often based on evidence from the U.S. alone. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI automates the creation of custom functional materials atom by atom
item.description: Imagine a construction site where the bricks are individual molecules and the "cranes" are microscopic needles so sharp they can feel a single atom. For decades, building at this scale was a laborious, time-consuming task where a single human error could damage the delicate tools. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Belonging, atmosphere key to attracting event-goers
item.description: Venues that become entwined in the cultural fabric of a community can be as enticing as the events they hold, according to University of the Sunshine Coast research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA rocket takes first multi-point look inside radio-disrupting clouds
item.description: High above Earth, thin veils of metallic haze drift through the edge of space. Known as sporadic E layers, these high-altitude "clouds" form from the vaporized dust of burned-up meteors, earning their name from the unpredictable way they emerge and then dissipate. Now, new results from a NASA sounding rocket—a suborbital research rocket—that flew five detectors through one of these layers simultaneously reveal unexpected complexity in the layer for the first time. Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers identify the world's first cell line with the KMT2A::SEPTIN6 fusion gene
item.description: Researchers at the Leibniz Institute DSMZ-German Collection of Microorganisms and Cell Cultures have, for the first time, identified a model cell line for a rare form of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). "The KOPM-88 cell line is, to date, the first and only known cell line worldwide to carry the KMT2A::SEPTIN6 fusion gene," explains Dr. Stefan Nagel, head of the Molecular Genetics research group in the Department of Human and Animal Cell Cultures at the DSMZ. "Thus, cancer research now has an urgently needed model system to specifically investigate this aggressive subtype of leukemia and develop… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new layer of the human genome: Embedded RNA marks may reshape DNA twisting
item.description: A new study led by Francesca Storici, a professor in the School of Biological Sciences and faculty member of the Parker H. Petit Institute for Bioengineering and Bioscience, has uncovered an unexpected feature of human DNA linked to gene activity and the physical organization of DNA. The findings, published in Cell, could change how scientists think about DNA organization, transcription and genome function. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope observes a giant, evolving, 10-sided atmospheric wave encircling Saturn’s south pole. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Scientists observe Einstein's gravity in the quantum world
item.description: An international team including Nobel Prize-winning physicist Professor Sir Roger Penrose has observed a long-predicted effect of gravity on a falling quantum object for the first time. The result shows that a fundamental principle at the heart of Einstein's theory of gravity remains consistent with the behavior of matter in the quantum world. The study, led by Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, the University of Ulm and the University of Oxford, was published today (Sept. 2) in Science Advances. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Weather shapes bus ridership, but cost and shelters can change the equation
item.description: What makes someone decide to take—or skip—the bus on a cold, rainy, hot or smoky day? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Animal-bone records reveal how cattle and sheep fueled medieval England's changing economy
item.description: As populations expanded in medieval England, key changes occurred in the uses of cattle and sheep to produce food and materials, according to a study published Sept. 2, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Matilda Holmes of the University of Leicester, United Kingdom, David Orton of the University of York, United Kingdom, and colleagues. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New nanostructure makes non-linear light conversion 72,000 times more efficient
item.description: Researchers from Graz University of Technology (TU Graz), Harvard and the University of Texas at Austin (UT Austin) have developed an innovative method for coupling light non-linearly. This opens up new possibilities for telecommunications and quantum technology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Principal support helps teachers, but isn't enough to stop turnover from classroom violence
item.description: An ongoing national teacher shortage has created a sense of urgency to better understand why educators choose to stay in their positions—and why they leave. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Whether you're an introvert or extravert may decide how you should use AI
item.description: More than a century ago, the Swiss psychiatrist Carl Jung made introversion and extraversion central to his theory of psychological types. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sorry, this neutrino laser won't work, physicists say
item.description: Neutrinos are pervasive yet intangible particles that permeate the universe, streaming through whole planets, stars and our bodies by the trillions each second. The elementary particles are often described as "ghostly" for their near-zero mass and elusive nature, as they have very little interaction with normal matter. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Weak sea-surface temperature gradients may fuel stronger tropical cyclones
item.description: The fact that the ocean gets colder as you go deeper is fairly intuitive, but a similar gradient exists along the surface of the ocean, even at scales of 1 kilometer to tens of kilometers. A new study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, suggests that this horizontal gradient significantly contributes to the intensity of tropical cyclones, providing a potential tool for better storm warning systems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dolphin-feeding tourism contributes to predicted dolphin decline
item.description: A study published in the journal Oikos, titled "Forecasting the impact of food-provisioning and other stressors on a marine top-predator population," found that without protective management, the Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin population off Bunbury would fall from 350 to eight over 100 years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When biology inspires mathematics: Hidden symmetries explain why widely used evolutionary methods can give false answers
item.description: Why do some groups of organisms contain thousands of species while others have only a handful? Evolutionary biologists have spent decades trying to answer this question using mathematical models that estimate how biological traits and environmental factors influence the formation and extinction of species. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wind-wave tunnel helps engineers dive deeper into ocean research
item.description: Inside a lab at the University of Texas at Dallas, researchers have re-created a small-scale ocean environment where they can make waves build, break and crash into one another. Fuente: Phys.org.
